utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Let me make sure that my microphone is on so that everyone can hear me. Does everybody hear me? Let me settle in. Let's have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say good afternoon to both parties and to the interpreters, of course. It's a pleasure always to see them, to see the Prosecutor, to see the Defence as well. General Blaskic. I believe that we have to finish with the cross-examination. Mr. Cayley is going to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. First of all, I think, for a change, the Prosecution and Defence can speak with one voice in welcoming Judge Shahabuddeen back to us. You look fighting-fit, sir. It's nice to see you back, and indeed, we are now offering Major Bower who has returned to be cross-examined by Mr. Hayman this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you, Mr. Cayley, for conveying to me the sentiments of both sides of the bar. I do appreciate your forbearance, and I do think you understand what happened and why I was unable to be with you earlier on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. We are very pleased to begin our work again. Once again, we're in our robes, and all three of us are here. The Trial Chamber is not unaware of the fact that the Defence has presented a motion this morning. Mr. Fourmy told us about it. In agreement with my colleagues with whom I spoke about it, I would suggest that we first start with the cross-examination of Major Bower. Then we hope that this will end at the time of the break, and if you agree, after the break, we could have a Status Conference which would deal with the problems that the Defence has raised, and we will also take advantage of that time to ask the Office of the Prosecutor how it envisages the end of the Prosecution's work in respect of the presentation of evidence throughout the month of July, but this can also be discussed in the Status Conference. Without any further ado, I believe that the Defence is agreeing, I think we could ask the registrar -- no, first, I would like to turn -- I saw you nodding, Mr. Hayman; therefore, I thought that we had nothing further to say about that. You agreed? Yes, you did. Very well. All right. We can now begin and have Major Bower brought in. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Bower.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a number of questions which I'll go through in the order of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At the request of the registrar, I would like to remind you, Major, that you are under oath. Since you had taken this oath several weeks ago, I am taking the liberty of reminding you of it. You are under oath for the cross-examination. When you are asked questions, please turn to the Defence attorneys asking the questions, but when you give your answer, please face the Judges. Since you apparently speak the same language, I would like there to be a slight pause between the question and the answer. This helps the interpreters and also makes it easier for the Judges. Thank you very much. Please proceed. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major Bower, as you may know, there is a transcript of your direct examination testimony.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If it is helpful for you to refer to that, you may ask leave of the court to do so. First let me direct your attention to your brief testimony concerning your visit to the village of Ahmici shortly after your tour began. Can you tell us when you visited that village?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was in the last week in April, maybe the 26th or 27th. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you briefed by the Cheshire regiment concerning what it believed had occurred in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was given a general description, but not in any enormous detail, but sort of an overview as to what it believed to have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone in the Cheshire regiment brief you concerning who they believed had been involved in the killing of civilians in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was general discussion as to which forces, and it was in no doubt that HVO forces had been involved. There was also talk of, I believe, extremist groupings had been involved, and I think one of them was Jokeri, but other than that, there were no individuals singled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were not advised by anyone in the Cheshire regiment that they developed a list of possible suspects, individual names, in connection with the killing of civilians in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said on your direct examination that you saw no defensive structures in the village of Ahmici. Would you agree that houses are commonly used as defensive structures during FIBUA, "fighting in built-up areas"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Buildings can be used when fighting in built-up areas, but they don't offer as much protection from weapon systems -- actually, trench systems but, yes, they can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm pausing for a moment to allow for the translation. I take it, because the roofs had collapsed on those buildings that had burned in Ahmici, you were not able to see whether there were spent shell casings within those buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some of the hallways and not all the floor areas were covered, but there was some debris on the floor, in the hallways from the roof, which did make identification of things difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you walk the perimeter of Ahmici, and in some of the wooded areas nearby, to determine if there were trenches or fortifications in any of those areas?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I entered into Ahmici with the Cheshire regiment, we were more concerned with the houses to the northern end of the village because they still had to be cleared, and it was in those houses that we were still looking for bodies and, indeed, found some bodies which were badly burnt, so, no, I didn't go up into the woods to the northern part. I had no reason to go up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it then your purpose in visiting the village was not to investigate the exact nature of the conflict, location of forces, location of any trenches, spent shell casings, and the like; rather, your mission was a different one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was mainly involved in the humanitarian side, the collection of the bodies and the repatriation of those bodies to family members, but obviously, from a professional military point of view, I was interested in what had taken place but, no, I was not interested in investigating the whys and wherefores of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you were not tasked to do so that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I wasn't tasked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your direct testimony that in May of 1993, you encountered the Jokers, or some members of the Jokers, in the vicinity of Busovaca; do you recall that subject?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding from your testimony that they were better armed than ordinary HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They appeared to be better equipped, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did your interpreter on that occasion tell you that she had information that the Jokers had been involved in the killing of civilians in Ahmici in mid April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: My interpreter, Dobrila Kolaba, told me after the incident that the Jokeri had been implicated in the attack on Ahmici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you know, or have you learned subsequently, what formation within the HVO the Jokers belonged to, that is, were they in a brigade or the military police, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: While I was in Bosnia, I was not aware as to what grouping they belonged to other than the fact that they worked alongside HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell me when you saw them working alongside, say, units from a brigade or a village platoon?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The attack on Grbavica and there were implications that they had been involved around Stari Vitez and Novi Travnik, this information came from the liaison officers, the British liaison officers, of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then I take it it's not something you ever observed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only incident which I observed was the attack on Grbavica, but as to what individuals belonged to what grouping, I was not in a position to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You made a distinction in your direct testimony between conscript units and a professional unit such as the Jokers. By that, did you mean that, first starting with the concept of a conscript unit, that such units were territorial-based and were formed on a village basis, that is, a local basis?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: That in itself is correct, but also it was based on the fact that the conscript element appeared to be made up of people who had served time in the former JNA or were just grouped locally from where they lived, and the professional elements were those that were held together as a formed unit and moved around the area as formed units and were better equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the conscript units include men up to the age of 60?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: That, I don't know. There seemed to be men of all ages. I'm sure there were some that age and some younger than 16 on both sides, but I couldn't comment as to their exact ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You offered testimony on the chain of command within the HVO in your direct examination. Other than your encounters with command, commanders and subordinates at checkpoints, did you have any other experience with the HVO chain of command during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only dealing with Darko Gelic at Hotel Vitez or physically on the ground when I needed assistance to gain access through checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information how either the Jokers or the Vitezovi unit fit or did not fit within the HVO chain of command you've described?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only from the fact that they were in an area that was controlled by the HVO. I don't know exactly who the sub unit commander was of that specific unit or how he received his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You also gave us on direct your impressions of the operative zone headquarters at the Hotel Vitez and you described it as a professional and efficient headquarters. Other than your description of being asked to wait for meetings and then being taken to meetings, do you have any other basis on which to evaluate the professionalism or the efficiency of that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: When either we wanted something from -- either access to Stari Vitez, we had to go to Hotel Vitez to gain this access and it was given, or when we were asked -- a request was made to us from Hotel Vitez, there seemed to be this air of professionalism that there was a known chain of command that people knew what to do if a British officer walked in with a request or as a result of a call to go to that headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you never met Colonel Blaskic during your tour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described an occasion in your direct testimony when you sought the help of Mr. Santic, I believe, and Darko Gelic to gain access to Kruscica with a food convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And did they go with you to the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had been at the checkpoint for a couple of hours, and it was at the request of one of the British liaison officers that we should, perhaps, go to Mr. Santic and Hotel Vitez to see if assistance could be gained from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they return with you to the scene where, I believe, a group of civilians, predominantly women, were blocking the road?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They came to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they able to clear the civilians out of the way so the convoy could proceed?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly the negotiation was headed by Mr. Santic, and he seemed after 20 minutes to have no luck in moving the civilians off the road. So after that, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the nature of the aid mission that you were assisting during your tour. I take it there were aid convoys sponsored by UNHCR and there were private aid convoys as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The UNHCR convoys and the NGO, the non-governmental organisations, Pharmacies sans Frontieres, I would classify those as sponsored. There were a number of unsponsored convoys, for example, the Convoy of Joy or independent aid humanitarian agencies would endeavour to travel through the Lasva Valley, but I primarily dealt with the government-sponsored organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that during your tour of duty, all UNHCR convoys reached their destinations?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you mean from the port of entry in Split to Zenica or from the warehouse to the actual town or village that required the aid?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's break it down. Did all UNHCR convoys reach the initial point of distribution?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The majority did, although it depended a great deal on what was happening to the south of the Lasva Valley in Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, that area. But the majority, once having passed north of Gornji Vakuf, would reach Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, when these convoys reached Zenica, to whom was the materiel, the food aid, and so forth, turned over to?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Zenica, the humanitarian aid agencies had their depots, their store rooms, where they would stockpile the aid until their field officers, representatives of the UNHCR, the Red Cross, would determine where that food should be sent. And it would be broken down into smaller, manageable consignments to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If it was determined that a portion of a larger aid convoy was needed in Kruscica, then to whom in Kruscica, if the convoy got there, would the aid be turned over to?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally, the aid agencies would deliver to two locations, either Caratas warehouses for Croat areas or Merhamet representatives in the Bosnian/Muslim areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your testimony there was a Merhamet warehouse in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Normally, I wouldn't term it a warehouse. It was a representative generally working out of their own house who would be the focal point for the aid agency to deliver the aid. And once the aid was delivered, they would, the Merhamet rep or the Caritas representative, would distribute the aid as they saw fit. It was that point that the aid agency did not get involved with physically handing out all the food to individuals on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I'm correct then if I state that UNHCR or the other non-governmental organisations were not in the business of delivering food aid directly to civilians in need; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They would deliver aid to where it was most needed, but they wouldn't physically hand a food parcel to one person. It would be stockpiled and then handed out by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about the private convoys? Do you know to whom they delivered their aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't say for the majority of them. We didn't want to get involved with the individual convoys. Occasionally, we may suggest where they should go, but it was up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How much aid was required by the inhabitants of Kruscica to sustain them?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't give you exact tonnage of how much aid was required, but because they actually had a resupply route from the south, they did not often require assistance from the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to assume that Merhamet or Caritas delivered aid to households in need; would you agree with that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't give a generalisation for the whole of the Lasva Valley, but, yes, the Caritas/Merhamet representatives knew who needed the specific items, whether it be baby food, medicines, water.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And food?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, food.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tonnes and tonnes of food; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The normal delivery would be ten to fifteen tonnes for an area. For example, the Vitez Caritas warehouse would get fifteen tonnes, and it would then be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Most of that was food; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, most of it was food.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the units you've described as conscript units, that those soldiers on both the HVO and BH army side, they resided in their homes, not in barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: When troops weren't at the frontline, then, yes, you could quite easily find people at their homes or in their towns. And they would receive food if food had been delivered to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Non-combatants and combatants alike; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: If people were not on the frontline, then they were to be termed non-combatants, so yes. But if they then moved to the frontline, if they took food with them, they would then be combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were aware that on both the BH army and HVO side, all males had been mobilised from 16 to 60 years of age, correct, to fight in the war?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware that the majority of the manpower had been utilised for the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You discussed in your direct testimony a dispute over the allocation of aid that was raised by one or more HVO personnel in Novi Travnik. Do you recall that? This was a threat, if I might further refresh your memory, that something would occur in Herzegovina unless aid was delivered to Novi Travnik; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was a briefing from the Red Cross that I had linking aid convoys from the south, Metkovic through Mostar to Novi Travnik and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that disputes over the allocation of aid between the Croat and Muslim communities were constantly being raised by both parties?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a source of constant bargaining. One side would want to make sure that they were receiving their fair share, as they saw it or as they interpreted it. A large aid convoy of some 15 to 20 trucks, even if it's just travelling through the area, can raise jealousy on one particular side, feeling that the other side is being favoured. So it was a general topic of debate with the aid agencies and the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was true of both communities, the Croat and Muslim communities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Both communities were involved in this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What happened with regards to the Novi Travnik issue? Was any aid blocked in Herzegovina because the issue was raised by the HVO in Novi Travnik; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Aid was blocked on the final leg of its distribution, but not blocked specifically in this instance travelling from Metkovic to Zenica to its central warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where was it blocked?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was blocked at what I termed the Novi Travnik T-junction. On the way to Travnik and Novi Travnik, there was a checkpoint there, and an aid convoy from Zenica was turned back. The normal excuse would be there was fighting and it was unsafe to travel the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that true?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The aid agencies, being civilians, were not keen and would not go into an area where fighting was reported. They had no armoured protection, so they would generally turn back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but on this particular occasion, do you know, was there fighting in the area that could have posed a threat to the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was fighting west of Novi Travnik towards the Travnik area, but it didn't stop the British resupply on the main route which we called Route Diamond, which was along the same road that this would travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that was UNPROFOR resupply?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the Croat hospital at Nova Bila. That was a church that had been transformed into a makeshift hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct that during the conflict, for extended periods, that church or hospital, if you will, did not have any water supply; do you know whether that's true?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there were times when water was cut off or the water supply was believed to be dirty or unclean, but not for any length of time. Otherwise, I'm sure we would have had requests for water containers, bowsers to be supplied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How about electricity? Were there periods of time that this makeshift hospital lacked electricity?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were times when the supply of electricity was cut from the main source. They had their own generator in which to power their equipment. And, again, they requested and received fuel from us to ensure that they maintained an electrical supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The makeshift hospital at Nova Bila obtained that generator from UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was or not. It wasn't given during our time but I know that there was a generator there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the makeshift hospital at Nova Bila when the HVO wounded were so numerous that they were put in the church pews because there were not enough beds to house them, that is, physically laid in the church pews?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: To utilise the space in the hospital, all the pews in the church had been pushed together and then mattresses laid in between. They made up the ward for the makeshift hospital. So that was how they housed the 120 bed spaces that they had in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you visit the makeshift hospital in the summer of 1993 when the ward you have described was full of injured Croat civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I visited the hospital on a regular basis, once or twice a week. And on many occasions, I would say that the hospital was full to capacity or, if not, two-thirds. The majority of the people that were there, I would say, were suffering from battle trauma, casualties, and, yes, there were a mixture of soldiers or men of fighting age and women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described on direct an evacuation that occurred from Nova Bila to Kiseljak, and then an airlift by helicopter from Kiseljak to, I believe, it was Split, Croatia. Did you also say that the wounded who were evacuated in that evacuation would have likely died had they not been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were a percentage of the number, generally the number was 50 or 60 and sometimes as many as 72, there was a percentage, 20, 25 per cent, that would die if they were not evacuated. The others were seriously ill. They could not receive the treatment that they required in the makeshift hospital, and there was no where else in the Lasva Valley for them to receive the medical help that they needed, that their injuries required. There were some cancer victims who, obviously, couldn't receive the necessary medication that they needed. So, yes, there were a number that would have died.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there a number who could not receive proper surgical treatment at the Nova Bila hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not a doctor, and I can't comment, but the medical and surgery procedures there were very rudimentary. I took the army surgeon from UNPROFOR there, and he was appalled at the conditions of the hospital and how the surgeons there had to work. So there were certain restrictions there which were imposed on the medical staff in the hospital. It was not an easy place for them to work, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're referring to the operating room which was down in the basement of the building?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were times when the casualties were numerous that it wasn't just in the basement that they would operate. There would be the old side rooms, I assume, where the priest would have offices or whatever, that most rooms were utilised for whatever reasons they needed to get people treated as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You testified that in the course of this evacuation you had a dispute with the administrator of the hospital or an administrator over who would be evacuated. Who was that person you had this dispute with?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name was Mr. Peric but I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that individual a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not think he was, but he tended to wear uniform -- military uniform during the time I saw him. Occasionally, he would wear a white doctor's coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it this discussion you had with him was interrupted when the hospital was hit by mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The conversation had just reached its conclusion when the mortar fire landed by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that mortar fire from the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We assessed that the mortar fire had come from the Bosnian army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the hospital hit?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The hospital was hit once, and two rounds landed close by, but the damage to the hospital was superficial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The windows were blown out on that occasion on one side of the ward, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was no major structural damage, but, yes, there was cause for concern for blast injuries for some of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the hospital marked with Red Cross flags and other prominent Red Cross markings; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember. It may have been, but I can't remember now, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From the time this evacuation of some 50 or 70 seriously injured persons was first requested by the Nova Bila hospital until the time it actually occurred, how long did that take? How long did it take to get BH army approval and cooperation to affect that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: This particular incident took 72 hours, approximately three days, to organise, but this was, I think, the third or fourth evacuation from Nova Bila which we had undertaken. And they seemed to be more complicated as time went on in negotiating cease-fires to get through frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you travel with this convoy over land to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We would accompany the convoy as far as what we termed the Zenica fly-over, which was the main junction towards Kiseljak, where we would then hand it over to the Canadian battalion who would then escort it, as it was in their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did the convoy go from the T-junction; do you know? What road did it take?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once it left our area of responsibility, I can't say exactly what route it took to Kiseljak and from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what route any of the evacuation convoys, you've said there were three or four of them, took on their way to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, only to the point where the British battalion of UNPROFOR handed it over. After that, the Canadian battalion determined the route as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why couldn't the helicopters come to Vitez to pick up these dying civilians and soldiers? Why did they have to be driven over land to Kiseljak to be picked up by helicopters; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know why helicopters wouldn't come in, probably the same reason why our own helicopters wouldn't pick our own UNPROFOR wounded up. It was too dangerous to fly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It was too dangerous to fly in the Vitez enclave; that was the assessment of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the British naval squad wouldn't fly in to pick our wounded up. We drove them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One last question concerning the hospital: Am I correct that other than the Nova Bila makeshift hospital and the Vitez clinic you described, there were no other medical facilities in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a hospital in Vitez, in the town, in the HVO part of Vitez, but it was a clinic. It had rudimentary abilities to carry surgery. And there was the clinic in Stari Vitez, and then there was the main hospital in Nova Bila that I dealt with. Whether there were smaller first aid posts, I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you concerning aid going into Stari Vitez: You said during your tour of duty, the aid agencies would not go into Stari Vitez. Was that because to go in they would have to first cross an HVO frontline and then cross a BH army frontline, and they assessed that situation as too dangerous for them to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some aid agencies would be a little bit more daring, take a few more risks. They generally would go into Stari Vitez if the situation allowed them. Again, they wanted to know if they would be safe. And specifically after the shooting of the UNHCR driver, they were very cautious. But if UNPROFOR could assure them that it was safe, then they would go in if they had whatever was required to hand at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that if there was a cease-fire, they might go in, but if there was active fighting going on, they would not go in?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. If the fighting was very heavy, then the aid agencies would not go into Stari Vitez. They would wait until there was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, to whom in Stari Vitez was aid delivered?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, it was delivered to a lady called Zara Halilovic who was the Merhamet rep, the representative of the Merhamet organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Unless I ask for names, you don't have to identify persons by name. Did Merhamet have a warehouse in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We used their or her garage, basement, utilised her house and some outbuildings to the side of the house to store the food when we unloaded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And then, I take it, further distribution of the food was left up to her?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, was there death or disease from lack of food in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Disease, yes, with newborn and very young children; but actual starvation, which I would associate with pictures from Africa, no, but the people were hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're saying there was no malnutrition, is that right, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the degree of what I would term endemic like in Africa, but, no, there was no malnutrition on that scale. The people were -- they were surviving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there such a thing as a sniper rifle that is designed for sniping, if you will, at great distances?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you be more specific with "distance"? Over a thousand metres, then, yes, there are rifles that are designed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what calibre shell they utilise, those types of rifles?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depends, again, on the range, the type. The normal 7.62 millimetre will reach a thousand metres, and one shot, one kill is what the British army uses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there a sniper rifle known as the Draganof (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did that rifle exist in Central Bosnia? Was it to be found there?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were briefed that this rifle was available to a small number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what calibre those rifles take?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that they are 12.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So a much larger sized shell than the typical 9 millimetre handgun?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's designed for a longer range than a thousand metres. It's also designed to pierce armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described encountering or being told about shells, much larger shells, made from fire extinguishers. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the maximum range of these projectiles?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Difficult to assess, but we believed no more than 300 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the average distance between the HVO and BH army frontlines were around Stari Vitez? How far apart were the forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the built-up area of Vitez, I would say that it was about that kind of distance, sometimes great --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: About 300 to 400 metres?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: About 300 to 400 metres, in places shorter, and in some places greater. It fluctuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where was it shorter than 300 to 400 metres, the distance between the two frontlines?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally in the built-up area of Vitez, Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In other words, if you are oriented with respect to directions, the northern end of Stari Vitez, is that what you're referring to as being in the built-up area adjacent to Vitez proper?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Taking a line of the main road from Stari Vitez, past Hotel Vitez, into Vitez town, to the south of that road, in that area, around where the minefield or the mines had been placed across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In that area, can you estimate how far the two frontlines were apart from each other?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: At some points, three -- 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How long does it take a mortar shell to land, that is, from the point of ignition to the point of landing? Does it take 10 or 12 seconds for a mortar, being fired at some distance, to land?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It can depend on the trajectory, but a crude mortar like that would take maybe as long as 10 to 15 seconds in time of flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about a normal factory mortar being sent some distance? Would it also spend 15 or more seconds in the air?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some mortars, which will travel six or seven kilometres, could be in the air for 20 to 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the time in the air depends on the distance the mortar will be travelling, in part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed. The further the distance, yes, but if you want a short distance, then the mortar has to go very high to come back down a short distance, so it can vary. It's all ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the fire extinguisher bombs be heard travelling through the air as they were catapulted, I take it, and then before impact?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was reported that they could be heard. I suppose similar to the V-1 bombs on London in the Second World War; it had a distinctive sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you observe any of these fire extinguisher bombs hitting a target or location, blowing up, and causing casualties, whether combatant or civilian? Did you yourself observe any of those events?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have to say that during incoming artillery fire, I tended to take cover and not look as to what happened. So I can't comment as to what actually landed and what went, what exploded, and what it was, but I was shown the remnants of casings of some of these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm certainly not faulting you for that. I just want the record to be clear what you saw and what you learned through other means. You said, with respect to Stari Vitez, the HVO appeared to be attempting to contain Stari Vitez. From Stari Vitez, could the BH army direct sniper fire or rifle fire, for that matter, on the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in certain areas, I think they probably did have line of sight from Stari Vitez to Hotel Vitez, so, in theory, they could then shoot at it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could mortars also reach -- excuse me. Let me pause for a moment. Could mortars also reach, if fired from within Stari Vitez, throughout all areas of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, in theory, yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know as a fact that the defence of Stari Vitez by the BH army also relied upon mortar fire from outside of Stari Vitez directed on Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the area of Kruscica and 325 brigade Bosnian army Preocica also fired into Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When the BH army fired into Vitez with mortar from those locations, what were the targets?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I honestly couldn't say what they were physically aiming at. I generally just saw the aftermath of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D38 (sic) could be placed before the witness? Mr. President, this has already been admitted, I believe, but we have received a French translation of the exhibit, and if it hasn't already made it into the exhibit files, we would ask that it be added to the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You said D38, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, D138. I may have misspoken. I apologise if I did. D138.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I only have the version in English here for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then, if I may, Mr. President, I'll tender the French. It isn't needed by the witness. If the English could be shown to the witness and perhaps put on the ELMO, I have just a very short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We ought to have us -- use a French translation for once. This is D138 for the in-French version. Could we have it, please, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There's a portion at the bottom of this exhibit which I would ask be put on the ELMO. There's also an upper larger portion which we won't be concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This, Major, is a portion of a MILINFOSUM which we understand to be from the 10th of August, and if it could be moved up a little bit more? I know this is difficult. It is on the very bottom of the exhibit. There are two lines. Those are the two lines we're interested in. There we go. Thank you. Major, this is a MILINFOSUM from the 10th of August, 1993, which provides, at the very bottom, "Vitez at," and then there's a grid reference, "a mortar mine landed in the centre of the town at" -- excuse me -- at 12/11.20. Is that the time, 12/11.20?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's the date, the 12th of whichever month this comes from, and the time is 11.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. " ... a mortar round landed in the centre of the town at grid reference 232924, which is controlled by the Croats. The round injured seven children, four of whom are described as VSI." What is "VSI"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Very seriously ill."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Very seriously injured," something like that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's termed "very seriously ill."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "And two adults." Did these type of incidents occur during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the reactions of the local inhabitants to these types of incidents, both on the part of the Muslim community and the Croat community? What happened to those communities when you had six, seven, eight, nine, 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, please. This is a translation problem I'm asking about here, when you said they were "very seriously ill" or "very seriously injured"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question exactly, Mr. President. I assume that the British term is "very seriously ill." In English, in America, I think we would say "very seriously injured" as a result of a mortar blast. We speak as an illness as perhaps the flu or something. But let's ask the Major what the meaning of this "very seriously ill" phrase is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you answer that question, please, Major, at least for me?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Britain, the medical services term degrees of life-threatening, whether it be through disease or through trauma, as "very seriously ill" as the highest, "seriously ill," and then "ill," as opposed to a terminology of "injured." It is terminology only, but I think it means the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Thank you very much. I've understood. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, when these types of incidents occurred, did you have any encounters with the population or learn from either the Muslim or Croat community, what was the impact on the population of having large numbers of children killed or very seriously ill as a result of, for example, mortar or sniper attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was actually in the Vitez hospital when this incident happened, and as you would expect, the relatives of the people who were injured were very, very upset and, obviously, there were some people who wanted retribution or revenge for it, natural human emotions. Certainly when children are involved, it affects people I think more than when adults are involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, during your tour, how many civilians in and around Vitez were injured or killed from sniper and other fire, either from Stari Vitez or from other BH army positions?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't give an exact number. When we first arrived, we thought we'd keep a count, but the count was too great, so we didn't bother. But it was a large number, I'm sure, on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to Stari Vitez, am I correct that the combatants in Stari Vitez were not housed in barracks, rather, they resided in private homes?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. When they weren't at the frontline, then they would go home to their homes or whatever houses they lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you know, would they also take their weapons, some stored munitions and the like, their equipment, and kit to their homes?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sure some of them did take their personal weapons, but when I visited houses, I didn't see rifles stood up in the corners, I tended to see people walking around, whether it be in Vitez or Stari Vitez, people would walk around without their weaponry if they weren't on the frontline. Whether it was because they had to hand them over because there was short supply or whether they just didn't carry them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, did the population move out of the houses that were closest to the frontline, that is, the BH army frontline, or were persons still living in those homes, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly the houses which were near the demarcation line between Stari Vitez and Vitez, people would move out of those houses, but there were some older members of the community who refused to leave their houses for nothing other than it was their house and they could be quite obstinate at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're referring to houses that were on or virtually on the frontlines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were within line of sight of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Meaning by that that if a rifle was fired at the BH army frontline but went over the frontline, those are the houses you're talking about. The next house that the projectile would hit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that civilians in Stari Vitez were offered the opportunity to temporarily leave Stari Vitez during the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understand that there was, I think, maybe three or four occasions that the occupants of Stari Vitez were requested to leave. Whether that was temporary or permanent, I couldn't comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described why civilians in Stari Vitez may not have wanted to leave despite the ability to do so. Is there a reason that the BH army would not have wanted civilians to leave Stari Vitez despite offers by the civil HVO government or the HVO military for them to do so?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't comment for everyone, but I know when -- the general feeling of the brigade commander in Stari Vitez, the Bosnian army brigade commander was that -- people didn't want to leave, but as the fighting grew heavier in September-October time, I think, he discussed it, but it never came to fruition. He didn't seem to give the impression that he wanted the people to stay. He generally gave the impression that it was because people made their own minds up. There were individuals, I think, who wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they allowed to leave by Sefkia Djidic or other authorities in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They didn't leave. Whether they were denied permission by the brigade commander, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that there was an implied threat, you felt, that if the third corps of the BH army ever attacked Vitez, there would be considerable damage to Stari Vitez. Was such a threat ever made, to your knowledge, by the operative zone command?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: On one occasion it was heavily implied by Darko Gelic, I think it was the 18th of July, when there was 30 hours of continuous fighting initiated by the HVO, we were negotiating to get in, and Darko Gelic stated that it would finish when they were ready, and if the fighting continued from the Kruscica or Poculica areas controlled by the Bosnian army, then they would continue doing what they were doing. To me it was a fairly implied threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the third corps of the BH army attack Vitez, just east, at least, of Vitez during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: At times, the Bosnian army to the north of the main transit route, east and west transit route, they certainly got very close on the high ground around Poculica looking down towards the Lasva Valley, so much so that they could interdict movement on that main route, which obviously was the main route for the HVO in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're saying that during your tour, third corps or other BH army forces cut the main supply route to the east of Vitez leading to Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They didn't capture the route, but they could hinder the movement down it by the sheer fact that they could fire directly onto it. I don't think they physically managed to capture a section of that road and hold it for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, during the time that I was there in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which ended in roughly November of '93?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your belief that the HVO had the military forces to defeat the BH army units in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, if they had wanted to, I'm sure they could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And yet during your tour, there was only one sustained attack on Stari Vitez which you described in the middle of July 1993; correct? One sustained attack on Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was not one in July. There were other periods of heavy fighting, but that was the main one I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were many other proposals within the HVO to attack Stari Vitez which Colonel Blaskic disapproved because they would have posed too great a risk to civilian lives in Stari Vitez? Do you have any knowledge on that subject, any information?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no information on that at all, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As a military officer, if you wanted to defeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you remain within the scope of the examination-in-chief, please? The Major doesn't have all of the strategies, nor does he represent the high command. He said in his principal examination he was a liaison officer for humanitarian assistance. We can't ask him for his opinion about everything having to do with military strategy, with all respect that I owe to the Major. I would like you to remain within the scope of the examination-in-chief; otherwise, we're never going to finish here. We could have Major Bower speak the whole day what he thinks about the war in Central Bosnia. So remain within the scope of the testimony as it was specified by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have concluded approximately two-thirds of my cross-examination. I have about one-third left. And I will move through it as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you then concerning another aspect of your testimony regarding Kruscica. With respect to taking aid into Kruscica, these problems you found at the -- I take it it was at the frontline or near the frontline that these groups of civilians would block the road and block convoys from going into the BH army-held portion of Kruscica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was the last inhabited HVO area before we actually reached the physical frontline between the Bosnian army and the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you characterise those disputes and those problems as local in nature, local tension, animosity between a Croat population watching -- perhaps a hungry Croat population watching 10 or 15 or 25 tonnes of food going past them and into BH army-held portions of Kruscica? Would you agree that that was principally a local tension or problem?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: To a degree, yes, but the arguments were what were used all over, but, yes, it was a localised problem for that small part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When Mr. Santic and Mr. Gelic came to that location on one occasion and engaged these angry civilians in conversation, did you get the impression that they were trying to clear the way for the aid convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were there, although the -- we were there for four hours; they were there for 25 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So was your answer you don't know what they were doing there or do you --

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were there at our request, but if we hadn't have offered them transport to get them there, I doubt they would have gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What else do you know about the involvement or attempts of the operative zone command in trying to facilitate aid convoys' passage into Kruscica, the BH army-held portions of Kruscica? Do you have any information about the roles or actions of the operational zone command with respect to that issue?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, other than there were times when we did manage to get aid convoys through, and that was generally facilitated through Darko Gelic at Hotel Vitez, and shortly after this protracted incident which went on for three or four weeks, we did get one aid convoy through, and we had utilised HVO headquarters to assist us in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So would it be fair then to generalise and say that the operative zone command played a constructive or positive role in getting that aid through to the BH army-held territory in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this particular incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a document I'd like to show the witness, Mr. President. There is a copy in B/S/C and there is a copy in English. There is no French translation as of this date. So they are together. First a B/S/C , then an English copy. So the exhibit will consist of the two pages, perhaps A and B, whatever the registrar would like, and I would ask that this be marked as the next Defence Exhibit in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document is D141. This is dated 1 June, 01-6-542 (sic), '92, and D142, which is the next document, and its number --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I interrupt? It's a translation. So if we could have 141A? Perhaps that might be clearer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right. "A" will be the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the English version could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, we'll need to read this quickly so that there is a site translation. This appears to be dated June 19, 1993, 16.10 hours from Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, 3rd Operative Zone, HVO command. "On the basis of the Agreements of The Joint BiH Headquarters, HVO 3: OZ command and 3rd ABiH Corps Commander, I command: (1) Ensure the undisturbed movement of the food convoy for village Kruscica June 21, 1993. The convoy will be escorted by the UNHCR, ICRC, and ECMM; (2) In order to ensure the food convoy to pass safely, make the temporary removal of the anti-armoured mines and other obstacles from the road; (3) The food distribution to village Kruscica is directly connected to the water supply of Vitez from the 'Kruscica' system. The commander of the Police Station Vitez is responsible for ensuring the undisturbed movement of the convoy as well as for preventing people to make any obstacles for the convoy. For the realisation of this command, I make responsible: HVO Brigade 'Viloska' Commander; HVO Special Unit Vitezovi Commander, Fourth Battalion Military Police Commander; Police Station Vitez Commander." Signed, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and then there's a distribution list. First, Major, can you tell us: Have you seen this order before in any language?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you have any recollection of events around either the 19th of June, 1993, the date of the order, or the 21st of June, 1993, the date on which the convoy apparently was to travel, that you can inform and enlighten us with regards to -- that might give us more context for this order?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The only way I could distinguish dates is if I have my diary. If I can look at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you ask the court. We certainly have no objection and would encourage you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, Major.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was around the time we were having difficulty getting into Kruscica, but by this date, I think we actually had done what we needed to do, and after these dates, I have nothing more to say, that I had problems or the aid agencies had problems going to Kruscica. The difficulties were before this date which is on this document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You discussed suspicions on the part of the HVO in your earlier testimony that aid might have concealed munitions, or at least that that suspicion was voiced. Were there any incidents within Central Bosnia that might have fuelled those types of suspicions that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I seem to remember there was talk that a video existed of an UNPROFOR unit that apparently had been seen exchanging weapons or handing weapons over to an army, but I can't remember what side, who the people were, but it was of some lengthy discussion amongst us. I think it may have been on national television, on CNN or whatever, one of those stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there an incident in Novi Travnik in which a U.K. L.O. team was involved in some controversy that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were a liaison team from Split, they didn't belong to the UNPROFOR battalion in Vitez, and they were reporting directly to the commander of British forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were in Novi Travnik, and because they were new in theatre, they didn't understand the delicacies of negotiation, and the situation moved some people across one frontline to another. Unfortunately, the Red Cross had been involved in negotiating this exchange, and it caused some problems for the Red Cross and I seem to recall that there were counter-accusations against this liaison team, that they had apparently been taking or exchanging ammunition or weapons across frontlines. But as far as I'm aware, the investigation carried out by Colonel Duncan, our commanding officer, there was no truth in this accusation. But, yes, they did move people across the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say "people," did they move BH army combatants from one location to another in their vehicles; is that what they did?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, for the actual people, what they moved, again, I would have to refer to my diary. I can't remember exactly who it was they moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did this event -- I'm not asking you to refer to your diary. If the Prosecutor wishes you to, that's fine, but to save time, I'm not asking. Did this event become known and become a topic of conversation among the local Croat population?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It did not appear as an obstacle during my negotiations, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it mentioned and discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a few days after the incident specifically in Novi Travnik, yes, but it was not a big issue as far as I was concerned or it appeared to be with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the death of the BRITBAT interpreter, Ms. -- is it Kolaba?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any other information concerning that event other than what you shared with us on direct? For example, was the identity of the perpetrator established? Do you know the calibre of the round involved, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the identity of the person that took part, but the calibre of the round was a 7.62, as we took the bullet out of the wall from behind her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what nationality she was?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe her parents -- I don't know which was which, but I believe one parent was a Serb and one parent was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about individuals you saw digging trenches in the vicinity of Novi Travnik. Did you have a discussion with your interpreter, Ms. Kolaba, in which she told you that some of the individuals involved in that digging exercise were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall her identifying Serbs in the digging in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did she identify Serbs as digging under similar circumstances elsewhere in the Novi Travnik or Travnik areas to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't recall now whether there were Serbs -- she would attempt to identify people by their family name. I don't recall Serbs being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall making this statement in your statement of 10 April, that "I have also seen that up in the hills, surrounding Novi Travnik, the HVO presumably forced Bosnian Muslim civilians to dig. I do not know what they were digging but it looked like trenches. My interpreter Dobrila also informed me that she saw Serb civilians amongst them." Do you recall that statement and is it true?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall that now, no. That was some years ago, I believe, that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me turn your attention to what will consume the bulk of the remainder of my cross-examination, the attack on Grbavica. Now, Grbavica is a hill or feature which was immediately adjacent to the BRITBAT compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have had placed to your right an aerial photograph, which is Exhibit 172, and we have placed a transparency on top of it. If it's helpful to refer to it, please do so. First I have some questions, though, before we go to the aerial photograph. Can you tell us for what time period you actually observed the attack? I asked because you said you saw the beginnings of the attack only. What portions did you see?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was, what I would term, the break-in battle, the crossing of the line of departure, the start of the battle. Once it was apparent that this was not a skirmish, a fire fight, it was, indeed, a battle, then all personnel in the UNPROFOR base went to the safety of the bunkers, and I went to the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, help us a little more, if you would. The assault started at some particular time of day. When?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I seem to recall it started in the evening time. From what I can remember seeing of it, there was firing going on, but I noticed troop movement, house-to-house movement, 5.00 in the evening, around that time of day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How long thereafter did you go into what you called the bunker?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I actually went into the ops room, and the remainder of the personnel went into the bunkers. I was standing in as the operations officer. I would say that 20 minutes or so I was observing what was going on, mainly out of curiosity from the front door of the British battalion base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How much longer did the battle go on during which time, I take it, you were in the ops room?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I seem to recall it went on through the night and on to the morning time in various degrees of intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During that time, were you in the ops room?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in the ops room. I then moved out of the ops room to one of the bunkers. I moved around as to where I was sent, as to what was happening in the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you spend, though, any of that time during the night or the following morning observing the battle?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, only the initial start of the battle, and then as it died down, the intensity, then obviously, the aftermath, at the end of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the 20 minutes that you did observe the battle, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was by the captain's house and the main entrance into the British battalion base. There was a bunker there. From there, I had communications to the operations room, so it was around the captain's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I approach the aerial photograph, Mr. President? Thank you. Also, I invite my learned friend, if he wishes, to join us. I'm going to mark the area of the British compound with black so that the transparency is fixed in location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, would you agree that the area right now I'm running the pen over without marking, that's the general area of the British battalion compound?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's the area of the British compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that's now marked in black; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you mark in orange where you were, where you saw these observations for approximately 20 minutes on the first night of the battle? You've marked that location with an orange arrow; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, my first question is: I'm interested in what portion of the village you could see from that location. I ask because the village is on a hilltop; correct? Are you able to, perhaps, shade in with red that portion of the hill -- well, first of all, could you just point, and I know it's difficult to see, point out the universe of the hill that is Grbavica. Can you point without marking so we can all see exactly how large the area is?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the high ground up here, and it slopes down to the road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that mean there's a ridge line of sorts running from the high ground down to the road?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The ridge line is like that. The hill, the contour, is a shape like that, so it's an oval-type feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the houses are located down by the road and a few on the hill itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There are no houses on the summit?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there were no houses here. They were on the high ground here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your earlier testimony that some of the houses were inhabited by Croats. Can you tell us which were the Croat houses or is that too difficult from this photo?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were two, I believe, right next to this main road here. I can't remember exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were BH army trench systems on the hill. Do you know where the trenches were? Can you indicate in a red pen, if you're able, the locations, specific or general, where any trenches or trench systems were on the Grbavica feature?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The trench system, as I recall, in this area, again, on the highest part of the hill, from what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the frontline was at the beginning of the attack, perhaps, in blue? Again, if it's not possible to answer any of my questions, please say so, but was there an initial frontline where the forces encountered each other, fired upon each other, during the beginning of the 20-minute period you observed the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: From that point at the start of the attack, it's difficult to say. From what I recall, generally, the Bosnian army had control of this side, the northern side of this road, and the HVO had control of the southern side. But there were HVO houses or Croats living in some of these houses dotted around here. So to draw a frontline, I honestly can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does it refresh your memory at all if I were to suggest that the frontline was essentially the main road running along what would be the base of the hill or the base of the Grbavica feature?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's pretty much what I would agree with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If there's no objection, I'd ask that we put, perhaps, a blue dotted line along the road indicating the initial confrontation line at the beginning of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As the battle progressed over these 20 minutes, what happened? Did forces move one way or the other? Did someone cross the road and go up the hill?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Primarily, what started first was indirect and direct support fire weapons, anti-aircraft machine guns firing in a direct role at houses, mortar, machine guns, firing in this area here where the houses are next to the base. And we could see the tracer went around us, support weapons around us fired, it has a coloured phosphorous flair at the back of it so you can see where it's going. We could see these, and we could see it going into this area here. So we knew that this was a larger assault rather than general fighting at targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did the BH army defend this line, the blue dotted line? Where were their positions and where were they firing from?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't give any great detail as to where individuals were. The bulk of their defensive positions were on the high ground, but they did use the houses as cover to fight from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The BH army, were they not, they were down in the houses across the road and were using those houses to try and defend the frontline you've marked in blue; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly the reports I was getting in the ops room after the initial 20 minutes from our call signs that were on the ground, is that they were seeing Bosnian soldiers down in this area here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a red circle or maybe a red "X"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Okay, another red circle?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: And here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And a third red circle?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
