utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's label, if you would, a "1" in the red circle on the top of the feature, a "2" in the next red circle you described, and then a "3" in the third and final red circle. You were saying that you received reports that BH army units were down in the houses within red circles 2 and 3; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were Bosnian soldiers and civilians down here. This is where the first discussion as to what we should do with the civilians started to come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And those are the same houses, correct, that the HVO were firing recoilless rifle shells into; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They tended to be going further up the feature to here. You could see the full shot coming in and also down into this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How was the HVO attempting to flush the BH army soldiers out of the houses in circles 2 and 3, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You didn't receive any reports on that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The general comments were it was intense, house-to-house fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would a recoilless rifle be the type of weapon you might use in intense house-to-house fighting to try and clear your enemy out of a house? Isn't that standard tactics?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: You could use whatever you had. If you have a recoilless rifle, then you would use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said in your direct testimony that some houses near the top of the hill were ignited during the attack and that you saw this. Can you indicate, perhaps, in the purple pen if you're able to, any houses towards the top of the feature that you saw burn or burning during the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I seem to recall they were up here in this area here. But as to the exact house, I can't remember now. This area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why don't you make a purple circle and put "4" in for clarity -- well, actually, you said you saw two houses burning, roughly, in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please put "2H" in the purple circle for two houses. You said one or two houses ignited down by the road during the time period you were watching. Can you point those out? Again, perhaps, if we use the purple colour, if you're able to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would have been around here where 2 and 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why don't you then make a purple arrow towards circles 2 and 3 to indicate that you saw one or two houses burning in the area of red circles 2 or 3?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can sit down. If we need to return to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I think we are going to take a break. The interpreters are tired. I would like it to be marked down that the Major has shown a great deal of hesitation. He's putting down circles. He's been asked a lot of questions very quickly, but he has marked -- demonstrated the uncertainties and doubts that he had in respect of these markings. This should be very clear. I believe that now the interpreters have worked for a long time, and we're going to give us a 20-minute break now so everybody can catch their breath. We will now resume in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please? Please be seated. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, thank you for bearing with me. I have, perhaps, five minutes more of questions. At the time of the Grbavica battle, did you know whether or not there was a battalion headquarters of a battalion within the BH army, 325th Brigade within, I think, approximately the red circle marked 3 on the overhead transparency on Exhibit 172?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say whether there was or there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had the British battalion requested both of the combating or warring parties to respect approximately a 500 metre no-fire zone around the base?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was an attempt to stop loose rounds or indiscriminate fire fired by two factions that would actually cross over the British base. And so, therefore, there was an attempt for an exclusion then of fighting about 400 metres in circumference around the outside of our base to ensure that we didn't suffer any casualties from the engagements between the two warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were some of the BH army positions you've described on this map within 400 metres of the base?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I honestly couldn't say. There were some on the top of the hill, as I've indicated on the map. As to the scale of the photograph, I couldn't say whether they were within that 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But the houses down at red circles 2 and 3 certainly were within that distance from the base; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed, and also right next to the base, but they weren't deemed as military positions. They were houses which people lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Even though they were defended by soldiers in the attack you've described; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was where the fighting started, so they were defending where the fighting initiated from. They were defending their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you discussed that answer with the Prosecutor during the break?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. All I'm saying is that's where the fighting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But that they were defending their homes, how do you know that the soldiers fighting in a particular home were defending their homes?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The houses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The structures?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, terminology, houses, homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were defending structures on the frontline?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether any particular event involving the death of a number of children a few days before this attack played a role in the timing of the attack on the Grbavica feature? I'm referring to the sniper or mortar fire incident?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: On which side? Who had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The deaths of a number of Croat children returning from church on a Sunday snipered or mortared from the Grbavica feature.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a large volume of sniping and/or mortaring from the Grbavica feature?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a two-way engagement, which is why we had the 400 metre exclusion zone. It travelled both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the area referred to as "BRITBAT main"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The area BRITBAT main is in black, the D-shaped location on the map. It's where the majority of the British forces of UNPROFOR were based in Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you observe any other portion of the battle or the aftermath, other than the 20 minutes you've described?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only, I would say, the toning down after the success of the mission was then the -- there appeared to be the looting of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So was this on the second day?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the morning. I can't remember which day it was. The fighting had ended. Obviously we had been up, I think, some 36 hours. So when the battle had reached its conclusion, the civilians had been evacuated by UNPROFOR to Travnik mid morning, about 10.00, 10.30. I can't remember the day or the date. It was the second day so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did the act of fighting end?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would have been sometime in the morning. Again, the exact time, I honestly can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you mean 10.00 or 5.00 or 6.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Early morning, not mid morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So some hours later, you had an observation of what you characterised as looting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, between, say, 8.00 and 10.00 in the morning, over that period of time is when we were finally coming out of the bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then what did you see at 10.30? You mentioned 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: By that stage, I was in my own captain's accommodation, which is when the soldiers came in, and we asked them to leave. Because by that stage, I had gone from the operations room where I was and ended up at 10.30 in my house, my accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many houses did you see items or objects being taken out of?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a general area, I would say the majority of the houses around where the British battalion officers were based, in that strip.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Down along the road?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Along the road bending round towards the main junction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would that include the red circle that you've marked 3 on this exhibit? That's the upper most of the two red circles on the road.

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not as far as that. I didn't see people coming in and out of those houses. It was much closer to the house where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said on your direct examination testimony that shortly thereafter, Croat families moved into a large number of homes or houses on the Grbavica feature. How many of these actions or events did you see? How many homes were moved into by, apparently, Croat refugees or other Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the houses that were habitable ended up with somebody living in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many that was?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly which houses were still in a fit state to have people living in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said earlier about the MSR, main supply route, from Vitez being cut. This road which is at the base of the Grbavica feature, this was also the main supply route to the Lasva Valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's the main supply right through the Lasva Valley, but it's not where I was referring to where it was cut. It was much closer to the Busovaca T-junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is another point on that same main supply route; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a point where it was in close proximity between the two sides. So there were times when civilians would not go down that road, but it rarely hindered us travelling down it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the HVO, the BH army position on Grbavica cut that main supply route; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and the HVO forces did as well. As I said, it was the frontline for both forces, and at different times they would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was the new frontline?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A little more slowly, please. I see that there is an interpretation problem here. It's hard to follow the questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Haste makes waste, and I'm trying to go too fast, I fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, after the battle was concluded, do you know where the new frontline was?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I can remember, the old position at the top of the hill was occupied by the HVO. But as to how far north of the main supply route that road went, I can't honestly say, but it seemed to take over that feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn any information during your tour of duty concerning whether any aid organisations or persons acting under the colour of an aid organisation smuggled munitions into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, for your testimony. Mr. President, we would offer Exhibits D138A, which is the French translation, and the transparency, D142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No comments, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No comments on those particular exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you any other questions, any other comments or things you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have quite a few questions, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Major Bower, during your cross-examination, you stated to Mr. Hayman that the conscript element of the HVO appeared to be made up of former members of the JNA. Can you explain to the court what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just that there were a certain age group who would have done conscriptive service in the JNA and were now serving in either the Bosnian army or the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're saying that there was a considerable number of the HVO who had actually done basic military training with the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: There would have been people who would have done training with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know how long that training period is with the JNA in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe the conscription term is two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, when being asked a number of questions by Mr. Hayman, you stated that you were uncertain of how the Jokeri or Vitezovi fit into the chain of command. And you stated that your understanding was that these units were in an area controlled by the HVO. Can I show you Exhibit D141, which was shown to you by my learned friend? If the witness could be shown that exhibit, please? Now, Major Bower, do you see in paragraph 5 that HVO Special Unit Vitezovi is referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, on the second line down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You also see that on the distribution, it says "Special Unit Vitezovi Commander"?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does that clarify for you a belief that you had about the command of this unit?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just understood that -- although not knowing who specifically commanded the sub units by name, but the way I understood it is that any unit within HVO Lasva Valley at some point would come under command of headquarters Vitez -- sorry, Hotel Vitez in some varying degree or other. Because that's where the central commander was, and the linkage between the two, the chain of command would obviously vary. But that's how I understood all the forces in the HVO Lasva Valley operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time it was Commander Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And who signed this order to the Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was signed by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a number of questions by Mr. Hayman about the aid moving in and out of the Kruscica enclave -- Kruscica enclave; I'm sorry about my pronunciation -- and you said that there was a resupply route into that enclave to the south. Can you describe to the court the nature of that resupply route?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: We knew that there was another route in, although as far as we could ascertain, it wasn't a metalled -- tarmacked road which would be like the road coming through Kruscica from Vitez, but it was a track which could be used, and we believed it was used, to resupply in small amounts. It was not a route which I travelled down, and we understood it to be a dirt track and not ideal for large trucks or vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: More suitable for resupply by foot than vehicle or horse, packhorse?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hayman, although, in fact, it wasn't covered in your examination-in-chief but it was actually opened out into your cross-examination, you mentioned the fact that helicopters could not come into Vitez because it was too dangerous. Did you see helicopters landing in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was a helicopter, a HIP-style helicopter which belonged to the HVO, did make frequent trips into the Lasva Valley and was a source of speculation as to whether it would achieve its objective and land and then take off again, and it did, during daylight hours, fly in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During your six-month period, would you say that it came in and out of the Vitez pocket frequently?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It came in over the six months. It's the actual number of times I couldn't say, but it definitely came in on a more frequent basis. It was the only sort of aircraft which we saw in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know what it was bringing in and out of the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It was discussed in our nightly O-groups as to whether it was bringing orders or information or, at one time, I believe Darko Gelic said it was some special equipment, but no specifics were ever mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether or not Colonel Blaskic ever travelled on that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was speculated when the commanding officer, Colonel Duncan, stated that he had left the area, that it was his way he got out, but speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, again, you mentioned in your cross-examination, not a matter that was covered in your examination-in-chief, that a UNHCR driver was shot in Stari Vitez, and after that, aid agencies became somewhat cautious. Do you know by whom that UNHCR driver was shot?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The area, the ground where the shot came from, was from the HVO part of the area. It was assumed and I believe the UNHCR made specific comments to the fact that it had come from the HVO element.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Around in the Vitez pocket. Very close to the east-west main supply route road from Vitez to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also stated in your cross-examination that when fighting was heavy in Vitez, between Stari Vitez and the HVO in Vitez, that aid agencies would not go in until there was a cease-fire in place. When there was a cease-fire in place, was it possible to gain free access into the Stari Vitez pocket from Vitez town?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there was still the checkpoint at the Travnik -- sorry, the Vitez T-junction which denied access and the mines across the road which were there during cease-fires or when there was periods of no fighting, and they denied access for humanitarian or casualty evacuation reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you refer to "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were placed by the HVO and it was the HVO checkpoint which stopped me from going in and also wanted to search our vehicle on leaving in case I was evacuating anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you frequently stopped from entering Stari Vitez even during times of cease-fire between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: After June, I would say I was stopped every time I wanted to go into Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, to get -- I had to go to Vitez to get to Stari Vitez, so every time I wanted to travel into Vitez, I was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you go to the Hotel Vitez to try and negotiate entry into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I then had to go into Hotel Vitez to then onward passage to Stari Vitez, and more importantly, to secure my exit if I was evacuating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were often refused access into Stari Vitez at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Around the time of September-October, when we were doing the evacuations from the Novi Bila hospital, Darko Gelic imposed on us, he wanted 24 hours' notice if I wanted to evacuate a casualty from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right --

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was hindered, as were the aid agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that a number of casualties actually died in that 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: It didn't help their condition. I can't say whether they died because they weren't evacuated within the 24 hours. I couldn't speculate. I'm not medically trained in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your cross-examination that the distance in some places between the Bosnian Muslim forces in Stari Vitez and the HVO was 300 or 400 metres, and then you also stated that the range of these fire extinguisher mortars or bombs was also about 300 or 400 metres. How accurate were these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were very crude, home-made mortars, so their accuracy was not deemed to be a factor. They were wholly inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did these fire extinguisher bombs often fall beyond the frontlines into areas occupied by civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed, and I stated at some points the frontlines grew quite close and the extinguisher bombs did land beyond the frontline of Stari Vitez into the more densely populated areas of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you evacuated a number of civilian casualties that were the victims of these indiscriminate weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I evacuated a number of civilians that had suffered blast injuries, shrapnel and blast trauma, and you can only get that from one thing, and that's from an indirect system that has exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- actually, strike that. We'll stay with Stari Vitez at the moment. Now, you mentioned, indeed both in your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination, that there were a number of civilian victims in both Stari Vitez and Vitez town proper. Where was the majority of those civilian victims: in Stari Vitez or in Vitez town proper?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: The ones which I dealt with were in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Bower, do you believe that civilians were deliberately targeted by snipers in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the civilian population were targeted, whether it be from snipers or any other weapons system. By the number of casualties which I ended up dealing with, there was no other way for them to be dealt with. I had to take them out. So the frequency of it just seemed to me that it was more than caught in cross-fire or circumstance. One or two, yes, if it was near the close fighting in July, but this was from when I first arrived in May till I left in the end of October-November. It was a constant source of humanitarian assistance they required.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the defence of Grbavica, and you mentioned at one point the people were defending their homes, and my learned friend made a rather unfortunate comment about something that he suggested that I had said to you. Can you explain to the court exactly what you meant when you said that people were defending their homes?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Basically, it's the houses. There didn't appear to be what I would call trench systems all around the edge of that road, but people were using the houses certainly in Areas 2 and 3, because that's where the fighting started -- perhaps I should have used "houses" and not "homes." But further up the feature, where the indirect fire was going, the recoilless rifles, the anti-aircraft machine guns and indirect fires, that wasn't at the initial break -- what I would call the "break" in Battalion Areas 2 and 3, it was further up the feature, and that's what I mean, that there was fighting engaged in those houses, and those houses were occupied by the population of Grbavica. I can't say whether there were soldiers in them. I would imagine if they were, they would fire and fight from them. I can't say whether they physically lived in those houses, but they would have used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you think that housing in Grbavica was targeted deliberately beyond the normal requirement of a military engagement between, in this case, the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't see the whole battle, so I don't think I could comment on actual targeting of the houses for any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, Mr. President. I didn't ask him for his opinions about Grbavica, I asked for the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I realise -- I'm trying to make this as fast as possible, but I gave my learned friend a great deal of leeway during his cross-examination. He explored a number of areas which were simply not asked by me in examination-in-chief. I did not object because I wanted the matter to proceed as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to stay within the scope of the cross-examination, Mr. Cayley, and try to shorten the questioning. This is a witness who has been testifying now for quite a long time. Try to remain within the scope of the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. President, I have now completed my re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Bower. I would appreciate your trying to shed more light on a few points, if you are in a position to do so. In your testimony, you spoke of the extent of Colonel Blaskic's command and mentioned that it was efficient and that he had a working chain of command which was completely in good shape and that they had also a communication system over a distance which was workable, if I noted rightly what you said last time. In the light of this definition, do you think he had firm control over what would be happening in Stari Vitez and in Ahmici, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: For Stari Vitez, I don't see any way in which anybody in Hotel Vitez could not know what was happening 500 metres away, and the fact that if I wanted to evacuate somebody from Stari Vitez or take humanitarian aid in, I had to go to Hotel Vitez and invariably speak to Darko Gelic, who was appointed, I understand, by Colonel Blaskic. So I don't see how anybody in there would not know what was happening, certainly when indirect fire was being used in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, speaking of Stari Vitez, could you in short say whether what happened there was necessary for military purposes or not?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: On balance, I would say, from the humanitarian aspect of my role, I would say there was no basis for denying me or the aid agencies access to Stari Vitez, and I think, more importantly, the casualty evacuation, hindering it, ultimately, is what happened; and I was not involved in the military aspects, I wasn't talking to the military commanders, I just dealt with the aid agencies and the civilians, and I was hindered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How did you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: If it had been just in July when the fighting was heaviest, the 18th, 19th of July, I could have understood that, but not as it progressed on until I left in the early week, I think the first week of November. It seemed to be a natural progression. It was, in my opinion, deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Deliberate to prevent you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: To make life difficult for the inhabitants. I think just -- I think it was sending a clear message. There was frustration by the inhabitants that they did not have the access to humanitarian aid which other people in other areas had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, as far as Ahmici was concerned, you mentioned that there was a majority of roofs which fell on fire. Could you tell us whether that was the result of fighting or of deliberate, let's say, putting fire into it and damaging it?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think I can say what started all the fires, but the fact that the amount of damage that was caused would denote that some would have been started deliberately, but I doubt all of it was started deliberately. Some would have been as a result of the fighting. But retrieving bodies from burning buildings and the bodies are fused to the wall because of the heat and hiding behind sofas would denote that people were restricted from leaving, and it was horrible, and that was in my first couple of days in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We had distributed to us a few minutes ago an order by Colonel Blaskic at that time, I think you also saw it, on June 19th, 1993, to "ensure the ... movement of the food convoy for the village of Kruscica," and the main point I want to raise is that at the end he says, "For the realisation of this command I make responsible" several brigades, including, for instance, "HVO special unit 'Vitezovi' Commander." Could you tell us if Colonel Blaskic had authority over the special units and the sub units? Were they all under his command?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I can say, as I explained earlier, I felt that if units were in the Lasva Valley, there would be some degree of control. It was a topic of conversation amongst the liaison officers with the commanding officer who had control of some of these units and Jokeri as well, and it was believed at some point there must be a link because these units would invariably work jointly, and it was assessed at Novi Travnik, Grbavica, and Ahmici. So at some degree then, yes, that's the conclusion we came to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, my last question is related to the interpreter who was shot by an HVO soldier under U.N. blue flag. There was also another case where a driver of HCR was shot. Was it also by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they both were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any complaint made to the authorities or to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the UNHCR driver, I don't know whether the UNHCR headquarters took it up, but certainly for the shooting of liaison -- sorry, the interpreter, I know that the commanding officer specifically made a formal complaint to Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he receive any answer? Was there any action taken?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe an investigation was started, but I don't know the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Major, I want to ask you a question or two about Exhibit 141A to which my brother Judge Riad just referred and which was the subject of questioning by both sides. Have you got 141A before you?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you are a military man, and I take it that military etiquette may vary from nationality to nationality, but that, nevertheless, a military man could identify a military pattern wherever it occurs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, when you look at 141A, which obviously was not written originally in the English language, would you be prepared, as a military man, to identify that document as a military document?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I think a military document, so long as it has a signature on it of a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would you look at the opening lines: "On the basis of the Agreements of The Joint BiH Headquarters, HVO 3 OZ Commander and 3rd ABiH Corps Commander, I command." You noticed a reference to an agreement between two sides. Would I be right in supposing that the reference there was to the authorities in charge of two opposing military sides?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Would your understanding be that the person who signed this document was holding himself forth as representing all the military forces on the side to which he belonged?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly for those within his area of control, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. I invite you again to look at paragraph 5, and merely to complete the reading by referring to the last two lines: "IVth battalion Military police Commander" and "Police Station Vitez Commander." Do you see those lines?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that the person who signed this letter was holding himself forth as exerting military authority over the police forces as well?

utterances.speaker: MARK BOWER (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that he's written "I command" before the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Major, I myself have no questions. My colleagues asked several. Thank you. Thank you, Major. You had questioning in two periods. I'm sure it must be difficult for you to refresh your memory in respect of your examination-in-chief of 5 June. Now you may go back to your unit and go back to your service. Before we authorise you to leave, we said that we would have a short Status Conference. I don't want to extend the interpreters' work too much, but on the other hand, I think that certain questions should be settled this evening. Third, I think there are some technical problems. I think perhaps we could take a 5- or 10-minute maximum break and then have a short Status Conference for about 20, 25 minutes. First of all, do the interpreters agree to that? I'd like to thank them. Now, Mr. Dubuisson, you need about five minutes; is that what you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It would be good to have five minutes so that we can have a closed session. I think everyone is very tired anyway. We'll adjourn for about ten minutes. We'll resume at 6.15. Major, please leave once the Judges have. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
